title: Nonlinearity and Mismatch
intro: Frequency response and noise are not the only limits on precision. Circuits bend large signals, and two transistors drawn identically are never identical. Both effects trade against power, speed and noise (Razavi, Chapter 14).

blocks.text: Nonlinearity means the input-output curve is not a straight line, or equivalently the small-signal gain changes with the signal level. It shows up as harmonics, as a deviation from the best straight line, and (for two tones) as intermodulation. Mismatch means two nominally equal devices differ by small random amounts; it produces DC offsets, lets even-order distortion leak into differential circuits, and degrades common-mode rejection.
Both are fought with the same toolbox: differential operation, feedback, degeneration, larger devices, and, when the physics will not cooperate, cancellation by sampling the error and subtracting it.

blocks.alt: Log plot of harmonic-to-fundamental ratio against input amplitude divided by overdrive voltage, from 0 to 0.5. The CS stage's second harmonic rises linearly, reaching 5 percent at 0.2. The differential pair's third harmonic rises with the square, reaching only 0.125 percent at 0.2.
blocks.caption: Differential operation removes even harmonics; what is left is much smaller for the same gain.

items: Nonlinearity: polynomial models, the end-point nonlinearity metric, harmonics and THD, differential circuits, feedback, capacitor and sampling-switch nonlinearity, compression and intercept points.
Linearization Techniques: source degeneration with resistors or triode MOSFETs, offset pairs, triode input devices, post-correction and local feedback.
Mismatch: Pelgrom's area law, the offset of a differential pair and of a current-mirror OTA, current-source mismatch, even-order distortion and CMRR.
Offset Cancellation: output and input offset storage, auxiliary-amplifier cancellation, and correlated double sampling.

blocks.text: Offset behaves like noise at zero frequency: it adds in power, its input-referred value is smallest for low overdrive in a differential pair, and the same techniques that cancel offset also remove low-frequency noise.

blocks.title: Which matters?
blocks.text: An amplifier must resolve 0.5 mV steps on a 1 V signal. Its input pair has a 3 mV offset and its end-point nonlinearity is 0.02%. Which of the two must be dealt with, if the offset is constant and the system can calibrate a constant?
solution: The offset is constant and can be calibrated out.
The nonlinearity is $0.0002 \times 1\text{ V} = 0.2$ mV, below the step, so it is tolerable; the offset only needs calibration.
blocks.answer: Calibrate the offset; the nonlinearity is acceptable.
